headline_marked: [[July Charter to be implemented]] for democratic, prosperous Bangladesh: Minister
headline: July Charter to be implemented for democratic, prosperous Bangladesh: Minister
summary: Liberation War Affairs Minister Ahmed Azam Khan vowed to build a democratic and prosperous Bangladesh in the spirit of the July Mass Uprising, marking the day fascism ended after 18 years of struggle.
details: Liberation War Affairs Minister Ahmed Azam Khan announced that the July Charter will be implemented to establish a democratic and prosperous Bangladesh, guided by the spirit of the July Mass Uprising. He made this statement on Wednesday, August 5, after laying wreaths at the July Martyrs' Memorial in Shahbagh, Dhaka.

Minister Khan described August 5 as a day of both sorrow and joy, marking the end of fascism after 18 years of struggle on the streets. He urged political parties, including the BNP, which had been active on the streets for a long time, not to become divided.

He further noted that the BNP government initiated a chapter of change in the country. The Minister also prayed for the salvation of the July martyrs' souls and wished a speedy recovery for those injured during the uprising.

State Minister for Liberation War Affairs Ishrak Hossain added that the government has not forgotten the July martyrs and fighters. He warned that any conspiracy to destabilize the country would be confronted with the support of the people.

headline_marked: [[Default loans hit 35-36%]], economy worse than thought: Ex-Bangladesh Bank Governor
headline: Default loans hit 35-36%, economy worse than thought: Ex-Bangladesh Bank Governor
summary: Former Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur revealed the true extent of the banking crisis and foreign payment arrears during his tenure, highlighting the challenges in stabilizing the economy.
details: Ahsan H. Mansur was appointed Governor of Bangladesh Bank by the former interim government for a four-year term. He had previously declined the same offer during the Sheikh Hasina government, citing a lack of independent working environment within the central bank.

Upon taking office, Mansur found the economic situation to be far worse than external perceptions. He revealed that the actual amount of default loans stood at 35-36%, significantly higher than the officially reported figures, which he had previously estimated to be at least 2.5 times the government's count.

A major shock was the outstanding foreign payments, with $350-400 million in Letters of Credit (LCs) and other international liabilities unpaid. This led international banks to reduce or threaten to cut credit facilities for Bangladeshi banks, impacting international trade.

His primary challenge was to stabilize the economy, which had been declining for several years with a rapidly depreciating exchange rate, rising inflation, and dwindling reserves. Mansur's first priority was to stabilize the exchange rate, believing inflation could not be controlled otherwise.

To address this, the policy interest rate was incrementally raised from 8.5% to 10%. He also focused on establishing good governance in the banking sector, leading to the reconstitution of the boards of 14 weak banks and holding them accountable.

Mansur recounted a strong debate with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) over fully market-based exchange rates. He argued against implementing it during a period of market panic and substantial outstanding liabilities, fearing it could lead to an uncontrolled depreciation similar to Sri Lanka's currency crisis.

While he aimed to bring inflation down to 7% by June, which was not fully achieved during his tenure, he successfully stabilized the exchange rate. This was a critical achievement amidst significant economic instability and international pressure.
